topic: sub:11|Formulas and equations|Medication dosages: Fried's, Young's and Clark's formulas

parts.latex:
A formula for the dosage in mL ($D$) of medicine required for a child aged between 1 and 12 years compared to an adult's dosage ($A$) is:

$$D=\dfrac{yA}{y+12}$$

where $y$ is the age of the child (years).

A 6-year-old child is to take 5 mL of a prescribed medicine three times per day.

What is the equivalent daily adult dosage of this medicine?

solutions.latex:
The daily child dosage is $D = 5\times 3 = 15$ mL.

Substitute $D=15$ and $y=6$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} 15 &= \dfrac{6A}{6+12} \\ 15\times 18 &= 6A \\ A &= \dfrac{270}{6} \\ &= 45 \text{ mL} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the equivalent daily adult dosage is } 45 \text{ mL}$$

parts.latex:
A parent used Young's formula to calculate the required medication dosage for their child.

Young's formula is

$$\text{Dosage} = \dfrac{\text{Age of child (years)} \times \text{Adult dose}}{\text{Age of child (years)} + 12}.$$

They found that the child's dosage was one third of the adult dose.

How old is the child?

solutions.latex:
Let $a$ be the child's age in years and $d$ the adult dose. Young's formula gives the child's dose as one third of the adult dose:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}d &= \dfrac{ad}{a + 12} \\ \dfrac{a}{a + 12} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ 3a &= a + 12 \\ 2a &= 12 \\ a &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the child is 6 years old}$$
